Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Friday, 23 February 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 009)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting_
Mr Dan Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Lachlan Gyles SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR MUSTON: Good morning. We're continuing with
Ms Rechbauer.
<CARMEN RECHBAUER, on former affirmation: [10am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR MUSTON CONTINUING:
MR MUSTON: Q. I am told, Ms Rechbauer, that you may
want to clarify one of the answers that you gave yesterday?
A. Yes. Yesterday, at the end of the session, when you
were asking me about the statewide price and the local
health district - and a local health district being able to
go below the statewide price, and doesn't that make it
lower for the state, I was reflecting on that yesterday
afternoon after I left.
The reason that we have statewide contracts is to get
the best price for the state, which I talked about
yesterday. Now, that takes time to work with the supplier
community in terms of understanding the disciplines around
that. So whilst mathematically, you're right, if there's
a statewide price and a local health district can get
a lower price, overall, you would, on the surface of it,
think that that would be lower for the state.
The reality is that once that behaviour creeps in, as
we go to subsequent contracts, the statewide price can go
higher because suppliers then know that they can go to
individual local health districts with lower prices. So
it's actually - in terms of equity across the system over
time, it becomes inequitable again.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. How do we know that?
A. From experience. So prior to there being the number
of statewide contracts in place, suppliers would offer the
same product to different local health districts and even
to hospitals within local health districts - some would be
paying a much higher price than others because of their
ability or lack of ability to be able to negotiate a price,
and so that's what the statewide price is about, is to stop
that type of behaviour.
MR MUSTON: Q. Can I ask you a few things about that.
First, so I understand it correctly, you say there's
benefit in centralised negotiation of the contracts,

because the state, as a collective, has a better capacity
to bargain with a supplier than would perhaps a smaller
LHD?
A. Yeah. That's correct, because it's volume based.
Q. So to the extent that you're talking about inequity
between LHDs or potential inequity between LHDs there, it
may be that one of them, say a large metro LHD, if they
were going it alone, would have a better capacity to
bargain than a smaller, more remote LHD?
A. Yes.
Q. So that's the negotiation aspect of it. The second
aspect of it that we're talking about is the price, is
consideration given to different pricing structures across
the different LHDs ever?
A. There's - there are always exceptions to - it depends
on what the product is. So - how can I best describe it?
In the standing offer of agreement that we have with the
suppliers, if they are to go to a local health district
with a lower price for a particular product, they're
contractually obliged to advise HealthShare so that we can
understand what that - how that will impact the system.
So there are circumstances where that would be
supported, but on a general basis, it's the statewide price
to make sure that there's equity across the system, that
everybody's getting the same price and there isn't that -
and to reduce the possibility for suppliers to be able to
charge more to one hospital and less to another.
Q. Can I ask you some questions about the items that are
on the inventory, so the Onelink warehouse items?
A. Yes.
Q. Those items are being delivered by suppliers to the
Onelink warehouse only, not to different LHDs?
A. That's right, yes.
Q. So in that case, it's a single, volume-based purchase?
A. That's right.
Q. And you are seeking to - once you have chosen the
product that you think is the best product, you are seeking
to extract the best price by your market volume?
A. Yes.

Q. Those items then need to be delivered to LHDs?
A. That's right.
Q. The price that each LHD pays for the item is the same?
A. Yes.
Q. Do the LHDs have to pay a delivery cost from the
warehouse?
A. It's free into store, that price.
Q. What does that mean, free into store?
A. That means that the price that they pay from the
warehouse is the price that they have. However, there is
a transport price applied to rural local health districts.
Q. So just unpacking that, if a metropolitan local health
district located very close to the Onelink warehouse was
buying a box of swabs, they would pay the price of the
swabs and what, if anything, for the delivery of those
swabs?
A. Yeah, they'd --
Q. What, if anything?
A. Yes.
Q. Would they pay an amount on top of --
A. They wouldn't. It's free into store.
Q. So it's free - for a metropolitan LHD the LHD is not
charged any money --
A. Yes.
Q. -- for an item to be delivered from the Onelink
warehouse --
A. That's right, yeah.
Q. -- to a hospital within the metro area?
A. Yeah.
Q. A rural or regional LHD that wants to acquire that
same box of swabs would have to pay what?
A. It's free into store.
Q. So there's no charge --
A. Actually, the rural local health districts do pay
a transport charge under the current warehousing
arrangement, and so that - yeah, that's correct. But they

get the same price for the product as the other local
health districts.
Q. So they would pay the same price for the box of swabs?
A. Yes.
Q. But in addition to that, they would pay actual freight
costs incurred?
A. Yeah, yeah,
Q. To deliver those swabs from the Onelink warehouse
to --
A. Yeah, depending on - depending on the product, yes.
Q. When you say "depending on the product", how is it
differentiated?
A. Look, that level of detail I'd need to come back to
you on. But there is - the rural local health districts do
feel somewhat disadvantaged because of that transport cost,
and that's recognised. And that is something that we are
currently working on for the new contract.
Q. If it be assumed that the rural LHDs are paying more
to have the items delivered from the Onelink warehouse to
their hospitals, they're paying more, in a practical sense,
for the products, aren't they?
A. Yes. But they're still better off because of the
statewide price. So even when you take into account the
transport costs, because they would have had that anyway,
because of where they're located.
Q. You say that. Can I ask, has any economic modelling
been done in relation to that?
A. There is modelling done by our --
Q. Who does that?
A. That is done within HealthShare by the category - by
the category teams.
Q. What form does that modelling take?
A. Well, yeah, I - I'd need to get that level of detail
for you.
Q. Do you know whether there is information available as
to precise levels of usage of different items at different
hospitals?
A. We know how much is used by each item, and the thing

that you need to keep in mind is that rural local health
districts are buying much smaller volumes of products than
the metros, so the benefit that they're getting is that the
price that they are paying for the particular good is based
on the volume of the state, which they would not be able to
do on their own, and they would still be charged
a transport cost.
Q. Who in your team does this modelling?
A. It's done by the category teams. So there is
a number - the products that are done are - so there's
approximately half a dozen category managers and teams, and
they are the ones responsible for looking at the total
contract and the service that accompanies that.
Q. We might have to take that up with them. It's the
case that you don't know the details of the modelling that
they do --
A. Look, I'd need to --
Q. -- or what the inputs or outputs of that exercise are?
A. I'd need to refer to the experts in procurement on
that.
Q. Can I ask you, then - do you still have a copy of your
statement in front of you?
A. I do.
Q. Can I ask you to go to paragraph 19 of that statement,
which, for the operator, is [MOH.9999.0009.0001] on
page .0006?
A. Did you say paragraph 19?
Q. Paragraph 19.
A. Yeah.
Q. I take it that in paragraph 19, that reflects what you
and HealthShare aspire to achieve? You're not suggesting
that those goals are necessarily achieved in every
instance, are you?
A. No. We - as I said yesterday, we're an organisation
that is maturing and we work on a continuous improvement,
and obviously things change in the marketplace, things
change in health, and we need to be responsive to that. So
I wouldn't say that in every instance we're perfect.
THE COMMISSIONER: No, I just read the first sentence as

at least partly aspirational.
MR MUSTON: Q. Can I ask you then to go down - do you
see three lines from the bottom, where you say "These
services help to achieve good patient outcomes"?
A. Yes.
Q. Can I just ask what you mean by "good patient
outcomes", where you use that term in that paragraph?
A. So obviously the goal of everybody who works in
NSW Health is to ensure that patients receive the best
quality care, and our role in that is to ensure that the
services that we provide work towards that goal, so whether
that be ensuring that, you know, the linen is right, you
know, is clean; that food is served --
Q. Can I ask you to focus on the procurement activities.
A. Mmm.
Q. Insofar as HealthShare is involved in procurement, to
what extent do you say that it is striving to achieve good
patient outcomes, or in what way? What sort of outcomes?
A. That we have the right product at the right price.
Q. Just pause there. When you say "the right product",
what is the outcome that you are referring to when you're
talking about a patient outcome?
A. So through our processes, our tendering and contract
processes, that we have engaged with clinicians
appropriately to identify the --
Q. I think we might be at cross-purposes.
A. Okay.
Q. I'm not wanting to ask about the process. You talk
about striving to achieve a good patient outcome.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. All I want to know is, from the perspective of
HealthShare, what is a good patient outcome?
A. That the patient leaves hospital better than when they
came in, so whether that be a knee replacement or whether
that be a bandage, that that has gone towards their -
a healthy outcome.
Q. And in terms of that good patient outcome, when you
use that term, are you looking at anything beyond that, in

terms of a patient leaving a hospital better than when they
came in, say, for example, longer-term outcomes for that
patient?
A. That would be part of the goal. We're there to
support clinicians in delivering that. Am I understanding
your question correctly?
Q. Yes. Could I ask the witness to be shown
exhibit B.016, which is [SCI.0003.0001.0023].
THE COMMISSIONER: It might be 16 is the med tech - sorry,
B.016? That's where you are going to? Right.
MR MUSTON: It is.
Q. I can give you a hard copy. There's also a copy that
you can see on that screen behind you?
A. Oh, that would be better.
Q. I just want to invite you to read - do you see there
a paragraph headed "2.1, "Current NSW Approach problems"?
A. Yes.
Q. Can you invite you to read that paragraph down to
2.1.1.3 to yourself. Once you have considered it, I just
want to give you an opportunity to respond to that.
A. Yes, I've read it.
Q. So just understand where that comes from, that's
a view being expressed by Paul Dale of the Medical
Technology Association of Australia?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you agree with what he's saying there in
paragraph 2.1?
A. No. No, I don't.
Q. In relation to 2.1.1.1, his suggestion that an
inappropriate weight is placed on the price of solutions
instead of using a holistic approach which capturing
additional value such as improved patient outcomes and
indirect costs to the health system --
A. Yes.
Q. -- how do you respond to that?
A. I think that's an incorrect statement.

Q. In what way?
A. I think patient safety and quality is our overarching
goal, so to say that price is - inappropriate weight is
placed on price, I would disagree with that. In terms of -
yeah, I disagree.
Q. So how is it that you say in its procurement
activities - I'm not talking about linen and shared
services at the moment, I'm just talking about the
procurement activities --
A. Yeah, yeah.
Q. How is it that you say HealthShare is using a holistic
approach which captures additional values such as improved
patient outcomes and indirect costs to the health system?
How is it doing that?
A. Because when we go - when we go out to market, we -
it's the process that we use as we go out to market and we
need to take into consideration what products are on the
market since the last contract, take into account the
patient safety aspect, take into account any kind of
service provision that might accompany a particular
product - I could give you an example, if an example would
be helpful.
Q. It would be useful, yes.
A. So hips and knees - we went out in 2018 and were
able - so prior to 2018, that was procured locally.
Bringing that together into a statewide contract, we were
actually able to reduce the number of suppliers and have
a more standardised approach to the products that we were
purchasing.
That contract came up for renewal in 2022 and at that
time, when we went out to tender, we also asked the market
what else they might be able to offer, and so a robotic
process was identified, which was trialled in Southern New
South Wales. So that was something that was - suppliers
were actually able to say, "Look, not only do we have these
knees and hips, but we've also - what is associated with
that is assistive technology in placing them into people."
And so that --
THE COMMISSIONER: I think the knees and hips contract is
referred to in Mr Dale's statement at 4.3.
THE WITNESS: So that would be a good example of where,

you know - I think is a very good example of where price is
not the overarching consideration.
MR MUSTON: Q. When you are considering tenders,
I gather what you're telling us is that good patient
outcomes, as you understand that term, is something which
is factored in to your consideration of which of the
tendering parties should be offered the contract?
A. Yes.
Q. How do you assess the patient outcomes which are being
potentially associated with the different tendering
parties' offerings?
A. So that would be feedback that we receive from
contract managers and clinical product managers in the
local health districts. So we have - when we have monthly
meetings with them, it is about not only the performance of
the contract but, you know, all aspects of that, which
would include the - you know, what is provided.
Q. Can I ask, with all due respect to contract managers
and clinical product managers - they're individuals within
the procurement stream?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Is that right?
A. Yes.
Q. To what extent are they, do you think, well qualified
to express a view about the likely patient outcomes
associated with using a particular product?
A. Well, they receive the feedback from clinicians.
That's their role. So clinical product managers are
clinicians themselves and have - that's their role in the
local health districts, to liaise with the clinicians and
get that feedback. When we ask for representatives on the
technical evaluation committees, they are clinicians who
are using those products, so there's also part of the
evaluation process before going out.
Q. So first way that you try and assess the likely
patient outcomes of using a particular product is to get
feedback from the category managers within your
organisation who, in turn, are informed by category
managers within the LHDs, who in turn, it's hoped, are
informed by clinicians on the ground?
A. That's right.

Q. That's, you would accept, potentially an imperfect
process insofar as it depends upon information being passed
from one to the other to the other, which is reliable?
A. But we also --
Q. No, just pause with that one. Do you accept that that
is an inherently unreliable way of assessing the potential
patient outcomes because it depends upon a chain of people
passing on information?
A. No, I don't - I don't think it's unreliable.
Q. Do you accept that that requires a chain of people,
starting with clinicians, ending perhaps several layers
through the procurement pathway at HealthShare, to pass on
information about their experience of price?
A. No. I believe our processes are very thorough and
that clinicians have good opportunity to be able to provide
feedback, and I have confidence not only in HealthShare but
also in the teams within the local health districts, that
that information is received accurately.
Q. But when you say that you have confidence, that's
because you assume it happens; is that right?
A. Because I know it happens.
Q. How do you know that it happens?
A. Because we meet regularly with the local health
districts and receive feedback.
Q. Who from within the local health districts are you
receiving the feedback from and having the meetings with, I
should say?
A. So we meet monthly with the contract managers about
the contract, and we meet monthly with the clinical product
managers, who give us feedback on the actual products.
Q. Is HealthShare meeting regularly with clinicians on
the ground in the LHDs - yes or no?
A. I would say - well, yes, we are, yeah.
Q. Who at HealthShare is doing that?
A. The category managers.
Q. And what's the nature of these meetings? Are they
a formal arrangement or informal arrangement?
A. Through the clinical product managers. So that's

where the - that's where the feedback comes.
Q. I think maybe I wasn't clear enough in my question.
Are people from HealthShare meeting directly with
clinicians in the various LHDs regularly - yes or no?
A. The answer to that question would be yes.
Q. So the meetings that HealthShare is having with
clinicians regularly, what's the structure? Is there
a regular structure whereby those meetings occur?
A. Well, I think the - the best way to answer that
question is that clinicians are there to look after
patients, so they have a support system around them to be
able to communicate to HealthShare if there are problems
with particular products.
Now, we - if there was a particular problem with
a product, then we would then meet directly with clinical
product managers and clinicians to discuss that particular
product. But if you are asking do we meet with them on
a monthly or quarterly basis formally about products, then
the answer to that question would be no, but we definitely
have relationships with numerous clinicians across the
state. So there are avenues for that feedback to come
directly to HealthShare.
Q. But those avenues would depend upon, to use the
example you gave a moment ago, clinicians on the ground
telling the relevant procurement people within their LHDs
that they perceive there to be problems with a product; is
that right?
A. They also have access to HealthShare.
Q. So they could also contact HealthShare --
A. They can yes.
Q. -- if they perceive there to be a problem with
a product?
A. And they do, and they do.
Q. Would I be right to say that that's an ad hoc process?
A. It's an as needed process.
Q. I think you told us a moment ago about, as part of
this tender evaluation - did you say there was
a technical --
A. Evaluation committee.

Q. -- evaluation committee. Who is on that committee?
A. So when we go - prior to going out to tender, we write
to all the local health districts and ask them to nominate
representatives to sit on our technical evaluation
committees.
Q. So is there a representative from every LHD on
a technical evaluation committee?
A. In some cases, yes. In some cases, no. It depends on
whether clinicians are available to sit on those
committees. Sometimes local health districts might be
quite happy to be represented by another local health
district. But they certainly are all invited.
Q. Do any of the other pillars have representatives on
the technical evaluation committees?
A. At times, yes. So the Clinical Excellence Commission
may be part of an evaluation committee or we use them as
a reference point for the clinical evaluation committee.
Q. What about the ACI? Does the ACI sit?
A. ACI from time to time may be as well.
Q. When you say "from time to time", what --
A. As required. It depends on the contract.
Q. When you say that, what's the trigger for it being
required that the ACI participates in one of these
committees?
A. So ACI is obviously the Agency for Clinical
Innovation, so if it's - if there is a particular product
that we require the expertise of the ACI, then we would
either reference them or invite them on to the evaluation
committee.
Q. How does HealthShare decide whether it requires the
assistance of the ACI in any particular instance?
A. It would come through the technical evaluation
committee members.
Q. So let me understand that process. The technical
evaluation committee is formed and meets?
A. Yes.
Q. And pausing there, that is the - the technical
evaluation committee is representatives who happen to be

available from LHDs?
A. Yes.
Q. And I think I might have not asked you who else is on
that committee. So you have the LHD representatives and
who else?
A. They can then draw - they can then --
Q. Just listen to my question.
A. Sorry, yeah.
Q. The committee involves people who have come from the
LHDs?
A. Yes.
Q. After the invitation has been issued?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Is there anyone else who are standing or normal run of
the mill members of these committees - someone from
HealthShare, for example?
A. Well, HealthShare is on the committee in terms of
running the process.
Q. Anyone else who would routinely be these committees?
A. It would depend on the particular product. So, as
I said, there are various categories, so it's very much up
to - so if you - if the question is in relation to the
Agency for Clinical Innovation or the Clinical Excellence
Commission, usually, the tender evaluation committee would
refer to those - so they may not be members but they could
actually provide advice into the technical evaluation
committee.
Q. So have I got this right, the technical evaluation
committee process, run by HealthShare --
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. -- sends out invitations to LHDs for representatives
to join the committee?
A. Yeah.
Q. LHDs will, sometimes yes, sometimes no, send along
representatives who are clinicians?
A. Mostly yes, yeah, yeah.
Q. Subject to availability?

A. Yes.
Q. That group then meets and decides whether it thinks it
might be useful to obtain input from either the CEC or the
ACI?
A. Yes.
Q. If so, advice is sought from one or both of those
organisations?
A. Yes.
Q. But if the technical evaluation committee does not
consider it to be something which is needed, then they
won't call for the advice of the CEC or the ACI.
A. That would be - that would be right, yeah.
Q. There is no standing arrangement whereby either of
those organisations have representatives that sit on
technical evaluation committees?
A. Not - no, not all the time.
Q. In relation to the clinicians who are sent by the
LHDs, would it be right to assume that the particular
experience and qualification of the representative depends
very much on what it is that is being purchased?
A. Yes, definitely.
Q. So for wound care items, for example, it might be
nursing staff who are sent to --
A. Yes.
Q. -- provide clinical input?
A. Yes.
Q. An orthopaedic prosthetic device, it might be an
orthopaedic surgeon?
A. Yes.
Q. Would that be right?
A. Yeah, yes.
Q. Do you know, in relation to the evaluations carried
out by these committees, how they go about assessing or
measuring the patient outcomes that are associated with
particular items - that is, the competing items? Perhaps
let me give you an example.
A. Mmm.

Q. Just so you can talk me through it by reference to an
example. You've got two different sutures. One of them
has some antibiotic product and the other one doesn't.
There's obviously a price differential. The technical
evaluation committee is called to make an assessment about
which one is going to be the better one to be purchasing.
Do you know how they go about evaluating the patient
outcomes that might be attributable to using, say, one over
the other?
A. Look, I'd have to - I'd have to take advice from my
teams. That level of detail is - I wouldn't be able to
accurately answer that.
Q. But insofar as you're aware, there's no formal
structure, is there, where particular outcomes are
identified and put forward to you, for example, at
HealthShare, so that ultimately you can form a view about
which of the two products is going to produce the better
patient outcomes?
A. That's the discussion that's held in the technical
evaluation committee.
Q. So am I right, the technical evaluation committee,
internally, decides which product --
A. Yes.
Q. -- will produce the best patient outcomes?
A. Yes. And then they make a recommendation as to which
suppliers and which products.
Q. Do you know whether the particular patient outcome
that they have relied upon as an important determining
factor is something which is identified outside of that
committee - that is, is someone told, outside of the
committee, who is involved in signing the contract, "This
is why we've gone with this product"?
A. So part of the role of the technical evaluation
committee is actually to, as a starting point, review how
the previous contract and suppliers on that contract have
performed and that helps inform them for the next contract.
So there would be --
Q. I think my question was, though, to the extent that
the technical - I think I said technical advisory - is it
technical evaluation committee?
A. That's all right. I know what you mean, technical

evaluation.
Q. To the extent that the technical evaluation committee
identifies, for example, a particular patient outcome,
which it thinks justifies going with a particular product
say, longer life span of a prosthesis or less
complications --
A. Yeah.
Q. -- to the extent that they identify a feature like
that as the patient outcome which should be given weight in
the tender process --
A. Yes.
Q. -- do you know whether they identify that patient
outcome to whoever it is up the chain who ultimately makes
the decision about whether or not to enter into the
contract?
A. That is the role of the category managers both at the
local health district and HealthShare to monitor.
Q. Pausing there, it's the role, but does the committee
actually communicate that to anyone? Namely, "This is why
we have recommended this product - because of this patient
outcome"?
A. They receive - so as part - being members of that
committee, they receive the feedback of that product over
the life of the contract. So that's taken into account in
their considerations.
Q. So when it comes to the balancing act of deciding
whether or not to enter into a particular contract, do you
know how the patient outcome is assessed in the mix of
factors that ultimately make up deciding --
A. That's probably --
Q. -- whether or not to sign a contract?
A. That's probably a level of detail that I'd have to
refer to our technical teams. You're getting quite
technical now.
Q. So let me just ask you at a process level.
A. Sure.
Q. I don't want to ask you about a particular technical
item - and it may well be that you don't know the answer,
so don't feel pressed to give us one if you don't know it.

A. That's fine. No, I won't.
Q. Is there some formal process whereby particular
patient outcomes are given any sort of formal weighting as
part of a tender evaluation process relative to other
considerations like price, contract performance, et cetera?
A. Again, I'd need to refer to the technical teams, but
it would definitely be - it would have - yeah, it would be
part of the considerations, I would expect.
Q. I think you said you would expect, but you don't - but
the position is you don't know whether they take into
account any particular patient outcomes in their assessment
of a tender; is that right?
A. I'd need to refer to our - to the experts in our
procurement team. I think that, you know, it depends on -
would depend very much on the product that we're looking to
purchase.
Q. Who makes the ultimate decision about whether or not
to sign the contract?
A. So the technical evaluation committee makes the
recommendation. That then gets briefed, comes through to
me. I sign off on the process.
Q. Pausing there, the brief that comes to you, what
information does that brief contain? Does it take
a standard form or --
A. The brief - yeah, the brief basically outlines what
the contract is, what the process that has been followed,
what the recommendation has been. I look to make sure that
the process has been followed. I sign off on that. That
goes to the chief procurement officer of NSW Health and
then he signs off on the recommendation, and if the chief
procurement officer has any queries, then it may come back
to the tender evaluation committee and then go back up.
Q. So I understand you check the process --
A. Yes.
Q. -- you check the recommendation? Does the brief
that comes to you contain any sort of discussion or
analysis of the relative pros and cons of the various
tendering parties?
A. It wouldn't go - it doesn't go into that level of
detail.

Q. So to the extent that the tender evaluation committee
has identified particular patient outcomes as being
a factor which may justify purchasing a particular item --
A. Yes.
